title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
carry: welcome it, then let it go
tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: two mothers, and a girl who rose into the sky. Today, Ganesha comes home again, and there's one thing you're not supposed to look at.

Don't look at the moon tonight. On the night of Ganesh Chaturthi, in a lot of Indian homes, somebody's aunt will say it. Kids look up anyway, of course, then quickly look down. Some grown-ups keep their eyes on the ground all the way home from the pavilion. Ask why, and you'll get a story about Ganesha, a big dinner, a mouse, a snake, and a moon who laughed at exactly the wrong moment. It's a funny story about something serious: what happens when you mock someone.
screen: `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.` → `A MOUSE, A SNAKE, A BIG DINNER.` → `THE MOON LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Here's how it's told. It's Ganesha's birthday, and everyone has brought him modaks, the sweet dumplings he loves. He eats every single one. Full to bursting, he climbs onto his mouse to ride home in the moonlight. A snake slides across the path. The mouse is terrified and jumps, Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly, stuffed with sweets, splits open. Modaks roll everywhere. Calm as anything, Ganesha gathers them up, puts them back in, grabs the snake and ties it around his belly like a belt. Problem solved. And up in the sky, the moon, who has seen the whole thing, bursts out laughing. Ganesha looks up and curses the moon: anyone who looks at you on this night will be falsely accused of something. In many tellings the moon begs forgiveness, and Ganesha softens the curse to just this one night a year. There's a sequel. People say Krishna himself glanced at the moon that night, was later accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka, and had to go and prove he hadn't. The Bhagavata Purana tells the jewel story; the link to the moon comes from later tellings. Why tell this at a festival about welcoming Ganesha? Because a guest in your house is not someone to laugh at. The moon saw a god fall off a mouse and forgot who he was looking at. The festival asks for the opposite: receive him with honor, even when he's clumsy. Then let him go.
screen: `EVERY MODAK, EATEN.` · `A SNAKE FOR A BELT.` · `THE MOON LAUGHS, AND IS CURSED.` · `A GUEST IS NOT FOR MOCKING.` · then, large: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small that's yours, hold it, and breathe. Think of a moment you almost laughed at someone you love, when they fumbled, fell, got it wrong, and hold them the way you're holding this thing, carefully, without mocking. Then, slowly, set it down and take your hands away.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth-day festival, the night many families keep their eyes off the moon.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. The moon learned that the hard way. Ninety-three down.

howItsDone: During Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindu families avoid looking at the moon on the festival night, remembering the story of the moon who laughed at Ganesha; they offer him modaks and, when the days are done, immerse his clay image in water.

notes: The moon story is told in many versions (in some, the moon mocks Ganesha's form; in some, the curse is that the moon wanes). The fall from the mouse and the snake belt are common. Confirm the version chosen and that it's presented as told, not scriptural.
Syamantaka: Bhagavata 10.56–57. The moon-sighting link is found in later Puranic/vrata tellings (e.g. recited as the Syamantakopakhyana during the vrata). Confirm.
'Many families avoid looking at the moon' — widespread, especially in Maharashtra and the south. Confirm.
Modak etymology 'often linked to moda, joy' — traditional; confirm or remove.
